title: Small-Business Website Maintenance Plan: Who Updates What After Launch?
description: Create a practical website maintenance plan with named owners, change triggers, acceptance checks and a downloadable responsibility register.
summary: Turn vague website support into a clear maintenance plan covering content, enquiries, access, accessibility, search checks and urgent fixes.
body:
A website launch does not decide who will update a service, test the enquiry route or respond when a booking link stops working. Without a maintenance plan, small changes wait for the wrong person and urgent problems compete with optional improvements.

A useful plan names the task, trigger, owner, approver and acceptance check. It can sit beside a small-business website design scope or be agreed after launch. It is an operating record, not a promise of search rankings or enquiries.

Separate routine, triggered and urgent work

Three maintenance routes with different expectations
Work typeTypical triggerDecision to record
Routine reviewA scheduled check of agreed pages, integrations or reports.Review frequency, evidence and who closes the task.
Business changeA verified change to services, hours, staff, policies or contact details.Who supplies and approves the new information before publication.
Urgent incidentA failed enquiry path, unavailable page, security warning or incorrect critical information.Reporting route, initial response expectation and who can approve a fix.

Do not label every request urgent. Define what affects customer access, data, payment, booking or essential business information. A new gallery image can follow the normal change process; a form that does not deliver enquiries needs a different route.

Build a responsibility register around real tasks

“Website maintenance included” is too vague to evaluate. List the work that may recur and record who performs it, who approves it and what evidence shows completion.

  • Business information: service descriptions, hours, phone, email, pricing statements and policy pages.
  • Visitor journeys: enquiry forms, booking links, phone and WhatsApp actions, downloads and confirmation messages.
  • Technical operation: domain renewal, hosting, deployments, backups where applicable, dependency updates and error monitoring.
  • Accessibility: keyboard use, visible focus, labels, instructions, errors, text alternatives and responsive reading.
  • Search foundations: public crawl access, canonicals, sitemaps, important URL status and structured data where used.
  • Measurement: search visibility, on-site behaviour and received qualified enquiries as separate evidence.

Connect the register to the account ownership record. The person responsible for a task needs suitable access, but task responsibility does not require permanent ownership of every platform.

Hypothetical example: a Varanasi tuition centre

Imagine a fictional Varanasi tuition centre with course pages, an enquiry form and a discovery-call calendar. This is an original planning example, not a SiteSutra client engagement or a result claim.

The centre appoints one staff member to approve course dates and fees. Its website provider implements approved content changes and maintains the deployment. The receiving inbox owner tests one authorised form submission after an integration change and confirms that the message arrived. The calendar owner checks availability when teaching hours change.

The plan treats an incorrect phone number or failed enquiry delivery as urgent. A new testimonial is not published until the centre supplies genuine permission and approved wording. A request for a new course page follows the normal scope process because it needs copy, navigation and search decisions rather than a quick text replacement.

Define acceptance for each change

“Updated” should have a visible test. A phone change is complete when the displayed number and link use the approved value on the affected pages. A form change is complete when validation works, errors are understandable and an authorised test reaches the configured destination. A new service page is complete when its content, navigation, metadata, canonical and responsive layout meet the agreed scope.

W3C’s Easy Checks include keyboard access, focus visibility, labels and error handling as useful first accessibility reviews. W3C also explains that preliminary checks are not a full conformance evaluation. Record the actual check performed instead of claiming that one automated result proves accessibility.

Review search evidence when the site changes

Google’s Search Console guidance suggests checking around once a month or when site content changes, while also noting that owners may receive alerts for new issues. Choose a review schedule that fits the website’s change rate and risk rather than turning the tool into a daily scorecard.

Use Search Console for Google Search impressions, clicks, queries and indexing evidence. If analytics is configured, use it for behaviour on the website. Confirm qualified enquiries from received messages or bookings. Google’s Search Console and Analytics guide describes the tools as different sources for search performance and on-site behaviour.

Agree the commercial boundary

Ask what the support fee covers: the review itself, a defined quantity of content changes, incident investigation, development time, third-party subscriptions, or only a response window. Record what needs a separate quote. Clarify whether unused time carries forward and how work outside the plan is approved.

A response time is not the same as a resolution time. Some fixes depend on a domain registrar, booking provider, email service or business approval. The plan should say when the provider will acknowledge the issue, what evidence they need and how dependencies will be communicated.

Download the website maintenance register

Download the small-business website maintenance register (CSV). It contains clearly labelled hypothetical rows and fields for the task, trigger, frequency, owner, approver, access, acceptance check, priority, commercial treatment and last review.

Replace the examples with verified responsibilities. Keep passwords, private customer messages and recovery codes out of the file.

Put maintenance into the website agreement

Decide the essential tasks before launch, then review the register after the team has used the website. Remove checks that produce no useful decision and add tasks when a real dependency appears.
